title: Gamma-Ray Attenuation Properties of Physicochemically Stabilized and Iron-Enriched Adobe Bricks: Experimental Measurements, Phy-X/PSD, and PHITS Simulations
content: The global expansion of medical imaging has intensified concrete use for radiation protection, conflicting with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), making sustainable alternatives imperative. This study evaluates, through experimental and computational methods, how the combined effects of physicochemical stabilization and iron enrich-ment influence the photon attenuation efficiency of laterite adobe bricks. The method-ology comprised: (1) selecting samples from three regions (Center, East, and West); (2) fabricating bricks with varying particle sizes, lime and iron contents; (3) measuring shielding properties at 0.662 MeV using gamma-ray spectrometry; and (4) determining shielding properties using Phy-X/PSD and PHITS within 0.04-15 MeV. At 80 keV, bricks with 250 µm particle size, enriched with 15% iron, and 10% lime exhibited a half-value layer of 1.06 cm, versus 1.6 cm for ordinary concrete. Iron, lime, and grain size boost laterite's mass attenuation coefficient only at low energies; density affects linear at-tenuation coefficient throughout. At 0.662 MeV, physicochemical stabilization and iron enrichment increased Centre Region laterite's shielding efficiency by 4.2% and 6.8% for 10% and 15% iron addition, respectively. PHITS and Phy-X/PSD simulations matched experimental results within 6% relative deviation. Stabilized, iron-enriched adobe bricks offer a sustainable alternative to concrete for radiology room shielding, supporting the Sustainable Development Goals.
